extracted.intended_audience: research mathematicians (especially combinatorics researchers), journal editors, and members of the mathematical publishing community
extracted.subtask_description: Evaluate whether general-purpose mathematics journals exhibit bias against the field of Combinatorics (using counts, editorial composition, scope statements, and editorial practices) and recommend tactics for authors and referees to respond.

rubrics_metrics.name: Count of Combinatorics papers (MathSciNet MSC Primary = 05)
rubrics_metrics.description: Use MathSciNet classification (search for MSC Primary = 05) and simple paper counts over time windows to measure how many Combinatorics papers a journal has published (e.g., 'Zero Combinatorics papers since 2009' for AJM).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The author used MathSciNet MSC primary coding to determine whether papers are in Combinatorics and reports absolute counts and rates (e.g., 10 papers out of 6544 for AJM until 2008; 0 since 2009). Note caveats about primary vs secondary MSC (see separate criterion). Long windows (decades) and totals (e.g., 528 papers since 1959) are used to make the absence significant.

rubrics_metrics.name: Editorial board composition — presence of combinatorialists
rubrics_metrics.description: Whether the journal has combinatorics specialists on its editorial board (lack thereof is an indicator the journal may repel combinatorics submissions).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The post argues that journals that 'do not have a combinatorialist on the editorial board' are more likely to repel papers in the area, and contrasts journals that 'found a way to attract and publish Combinatorics papers' by including such representation.

rubrics_metrics.name: Journal scope statement versus actual subject distribution
rubrics_metrics.description: Compare a journal's stated scope (e.g., 'publish papers of the highest quality, spanning the range of mathematics') with the empirical distribution of areas it publishes to detect mismatch.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use ZbMATH/other breakdowns of top areas to see skew (example: CJM claimed to span range but 2/3 of papers are in just two areas). If the distribution concentrates heavily in a few fields, the 'spanning the range' claim is not borne out.

rubrics_metrics.name: Editorial bias (explicit or implicit) against Combinatorics
rubrics_metrics.description: Evidence that editors or journal policies systematically deprioritize Combinatorics (explicit bias, internal policy, or practices leading to zero publications in the field).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples: editor replies claiming 'no bias' despite zero publications; the post calls this an indicator of a problem and suggests journals may 'have an explicit bias, not having a combinatorialist on the editorial board, never encouraging best people in the area to submit, or using random people to give “quick opinions” on work far away from their area of expertise.'

rubrics_metrics.name: Use of quick or out-of-area opinions for refereeing
rubrics_metrics.description: Journals that rely on rapid opinions from referees outside the paper's area risk misjudging subject-specific work and thereby rejecting or discouraging that field's submissions.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The author hypothesizes that some journals 'use random people to give “quick opinions” on work far away from their area of expertise' which can repel submissions from specialized fields like Combinatorics.

rubrics_metrics.name: Backlog / 'major open problem' rejection practice
rubrics_metrics.description: Editors using backlog or restricting new submissions except for solutions to 'major open problems' as a reason to reject submissions in certain areas.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The post reproduces an editor's rejection saying the journal 'decided ... not to take any new submissions for the next few months, except possibly for the solution of a major open problem,' and treats this as an example of gatekeeping that can disproportionately exclude certain areas.

rubrics_metrics.name: Grandfathered areas limiting topical diversity
rubrics_metrics.description: The idea that journals may have entrenched favored areas ('grandfathered areas') which occupy most slots and leave little room for other fields.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Author suggests that with enormous submission growth, journals may keep publishing in established areas making it harder for other fields to gain representation; check long-term composition to detect this.

rubrics_metrics.name: Author coding practices affect measurement (primary vs secondary MSC)
rubrics_metrics.description: Authors sometimes list Combinatorics as a secondary MSC rather than primary, which will undercount combinatorics presence if only primary MSC is used.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Stephen Griffeth's comment is cited: there are combinatorics-related papers where combinatorics appears as a secondary MSC; therefore counts using only primary MSC can misrepresent the true amount of combinatorial content. This is a measurement caveat to bear in mind.

rubrics_metrics.name: Definition norm: use MSC=05 as concrete proxy for Combinatorics
rubrics_metrics.description: Adopt a clear, computable definition for what counts as Combinatorics (the author uses MSC Primary = 05) rather than relying on informal or variable self-identification.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Author notes MSC=05 is imperfect but provides concrete, computable, and precise criteria to determine whether a paper is in Combinatorics; warns that without definition 'everything is Combinatorics' and comparisons become meaningless.

rubrics_metrics.name: Transparency of editorial decision-making (voting rules, acceptance processes)
rubrics_metrics.description: Whether acceptance decisions are individual, majority, or unanimous and how much transparency there is about this process; lack of transparency can hide systemic exclusion.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The author questions whether 'any editor accept any paper they wish or the decision has to be made by a majority of editors? Or, perhaps, each paper is accepted only by a unanimous vote?' and points out lack of answers makes it hard to diagnose rejection patterns.

rubrics_metrics.name: Long-term selectivity evidence via time-window analysis
rubrics_metrics.description: Use long time-window statistics (decades or since journal founding) and contextual totals (total papers published) to judge whether absence of combinatorics work is statistically meaningful.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples in the post: Publ. Math. IHÉS — 528 papers since 1959 and zero combinatorics; showing absolute zero over long periods plus sizable totals strengthens the claim of exclusion.

rubrics_metrics.name: Scope wording that excludes 'non-pure' or 'not highest quality' work
rubrics_metrics.description: Journal scope language (e.g., 'emphasis on pure mathematics' or 'papers of the highest quality') can be used—explicitly or implicitly—to exclude areas perceived as not matching those labels.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: CJM's claim to emphasize 'pure mathematics' is contrasted with zero combinatorics papers; the author suggests that such wording can be applied selectively to exclude certain fields.

rubrics_metrics.name: Advice for authors: submit best work (especially if tenured) rather than boycott
rubrics_metrics.description: Recommended tactical response: combinatorialists should consider submitting their best work to the journals in question (particularly if they are tenured), rather than organizing boycotts.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The author explicitly advises 'Please don’t boycott them — it’s counterproductive' and recommends submitting best work as a way to change editorial behavior over time.

rubrics_metrics.name: Accountability tactic for referees: ask about bias and follow up on outcomes
rubrics_metrics.description: When asked to referee or give a quick opinion, interrogate the editor about potential bias and follow up if you give a positive opinion to confirm whether the paper was accepted.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Specific recommended lines: ask the editor 'Does your journal have a bias against Combinatorics?'; if you write a positive report, follow up and ask if the paper is accepted, and if not, challenge the editor's denial of bias. Aim to 'exhaust them' as a form of accountability.

rubrics_metrics.name: Advocacy tactic: shame journals and mobilize community pressure
rubrics_metrics.description: Use public shaming and community discussion to pressure journals to explain or change editorial practices.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Suggestions include telling colleagues that the journals have an anti-Combinatorics bias, sending links to editorial board members and asking them to write a comment, and generally publicizing the issue to create pressure for explanation and change.
